candidates.title: The Runner has no load test, though the rules and CI require one
candidates.text:
The Python rules require a `tests/load/` test for code on concurrency or environment-layer paths, asserting latency, throughput, or resource bounds. CI runs that tier as its own step (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:54`). This slice adds a tick budget, detached `sq` launches, and per-project polling, and none of it has a load test. `tests/load/` covers crash loops, recovery scale, and concurrent inbox writes, but not the Runner. The slice document does not mention load tests or record a waiver.

Add a load test with several projects and a realistic run count that asserts the tick deadline holds and `sq` calls per interval stay bounded. It would also have caught the shared-observer finding above. If the PM accepts a deferral, record it in the slice.

candidates.title: Repeated unexpected faults can busy-loop the resident process
candidates.text: The exception handler always reports work after escalating. But escalation may write nothing when the node is already blocked or the project escalation is already open (`src/amoeba/runner/faults.py:171-190`). The host waits for its idle interval only when no tenant reports work (`src/amoeba/process/host.py:251-254`), so a recurring planner or stage exception can make the Runner retry continuously and consume CPU. Report work only when escalation actually changed state, or otherwise allow the host to idle.

candidates.title: Repeated unexpected faults bypass the idle interval
candidates.text: The exception handler always reports a write, even when `escalate` deduplicates an existing escalation or finds an already-blocked node. `ResidentProcess._loop` waits only when tenants report no work, so a persistent exception produces a tight retry-and-error-log loop. Have escalation report whether it actually changed the store, and combine that with `tick.wrote` instead of returning unconditional `True`.

candidates.title: Visible-range effect is gated on a ref that is not a dependency, so the advertised seam does not activate on the first series
candidates.text:
The effect reads `seriesCountRef.current === 0` as its data guard but lists only `[mount.ready, chart, range]` as dependencies. `seriesCountRef` is a ref (src/chart/use-chart-provider.ts:72), written by `series.onAdded`/`onRemoved` (lines 147–151); writing it does not re-render and cannot re-run an effect. So when the count goes 0 → 1 while `range` is unchanged, the effect does not re-run and `chart.setVisibleRange(range)` is never issued.

The comment at lines 328–338 asserts "The effect and its dependency array stay wired as the seam initiative 120 activates the moment it adds the first series." That is not what the code does: it activates on the *next* range change after a series exists. The initiative-120 flow this seam is built for (range set → data fetched → `addSeries`) would therefore apply the range only if the range happens to change again afterwards. The test that appears to cover this, `src/test/use-chart-provider.translation.test.tsx:135-145` ("applies the range once a series exists"), passes only because it calls `setRange` *after* `addSeries` — it exercises the incidental ordering, not the claim in the comment. The current-slice behaviour is still correct (the chart is empty by design, so the call is always withheld), which is why this is a CONCERN rather than a FAIL.

candidates.title: Run-id extraction from a journal entry is duplicated three times, with different strictness
candidates.text:
The same rule, that an `sq_run` entry must carry a non-empty string `run_id`, is written separately in three places:
- `observe.py:127-129` in `_observe_one` raises `ValueError` on a missing or empty id.
- `finish.py:141-145` in `_run_id` raises `ValueError` only when the id is not a string. An empty string passes.
- `launch.py:166` `_text_parameter(entry, PARAM_RUN_ID)` raises on a missing or empty id.

`faults.py:194-198` in `_in_flight_run_ids` skips validation and calls `str(entry.parameters[PARAM_RUN_ID])`. That raises `KeyError` for a malformed entry. It does this inside `escalate`, which is the last-resort fault path, so the failure surfaces from the one place that must not raise. The project rules say not to duplicate logic and not to scatter comparison values.

Define one helper, for example `run_id_of(entry)`, in one module (probably `launch.py`) that raises `ValueError`. Use it in `observe`, `finish` and `faults`. For `escalate`, decide explicitly what a malformed entry means.

candidates.text:
```python
str(entry.parameters[PARAM_RUN_ID])
```

Every sibling that reads the same key defends itself and raises a descriptive error: `launch._text_parameter` and `finish._run_id` use `.get` plus an explicit `ValueError`, and `observe._observe_one` does the same for the same key. `REQUIRED_PARAMETER_KEYS` guarantees the key only for entries written through today's `journal_issue`; `ProcessSettings` documents entries "journaled before slice 120, which carry no run id", and `unresolved_journal_entries` returns whatever is unresolved. A bare `KeyError` here propagates out of `escalate`, which the comment in `_tick_project` explicitly says is "not caught again", turning a per-project fault into a process-wide crash with a traceback at the CLI boundary. Use `.get` and raise the descriptive error the other readers raise.

candidates.title: `_in_flight_run_ids` indexes `parameters["run_id"]` directly, inside the handler that must not raise
candidates.text:
```python
return [
    str(entry.parameters[PARAM_RUN_ID])
    for entry in store.unresolved_journal_entries(project_id)
    if entry.node_id == node_id and entry.kind is CommandKind.SQ_RUN
]
```

`escalate` is called from the one broad `except` in `RunnerTenant._tick_project`, after the original fault has already been logged. A `KeyError` raised here is not caught anywhere: it escapes `_tick_project`, ends the tenant's tick, and takes the process down instead of escalating, which is the opposite of the "expected faults are answers, not exceptions" doctrine stated in `faults.py`'s own module docstring. The sibling readers are careful about exactly this value — `observe._observe_one` and `finish._run_id` both treat an unusable run id as an explicit `ValueError` with a message naming the entry — so the bare subscript is inconsistent within the same stage. It is reachable when an unresolved `sq_run` entry carries no `run_id` key (pre-slice-120 rows are the documented case); recovery normally resolves or escalates those before tenants tick, so this is narrow, but the failure mode is a crash rather than an answer. Using `.get` plus the same "unusable run id" message would make the handler total.

candidates.title: Expected faults lose detail: first payload wins, and each recurring fault costs a write
candidates.text: `raise_expected_faults` calls `store.raise_project_escalation` once per fault. The store returns an already-open row unchanged (src/amoeba/store/project_escalations.py:58-59), so the escalation keeps the payload of the first fault of that kind ever raised. Two `run_observation_failed` faults for different runs in one tick: the second run's id and detail are dropped. A `launch_overdue` escalation keeps the stderr tail from when it first opened, so an operator sees stale evidence. Each recurring fault also opens a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` write transaction every tick even when nothing is written. Fix: update the open row's payload, or raise once per kind with the current details, and skip the store call for kinds already open this tick.

candidates.title: Repeated unexpected faults can busy-loop the resident process
candidates.text: The exception handler always reports work after escalating. But escalation may write nothing when the node is already blocked or the project escalation is already open (`src/amoeba/runner/faults.py:171-190`). The host waits for its idle interval only when no tenant reports work (`src/amoeba/process/host.py:251-254`), so a recurring planner or stage exception can make the Runner retry continuously and consume CPU. candidates.title: Repeated unexpected faults bypass the idle interval

candidates.title: Escalation path can itself raise on a malformed run id
candidates.text: `_in_flight_run_ids` reads `entry.parameters[PARAM_RUN_ID]` with a hard subscript and wraps it in `str()`. `RunObserver._observe_one` and `finish._run_id` both raise `ValueError` when the run id is missing, empty or not a string. candidates.title: Project-scoped escalations keep only the first fault of each kind
candidates.text: The store deduplicates on `(project, kind)`. If two runs go `launch_overdue` or `run_observation_failed` in the same project, only the first fault's `node_id`, `run_id` and `detail` reach the escalation. The second node's failure is invisible to the operator until the first clears. `TickFaults` holds every fault, so the loss happens when the rows are written. Aggregate the details into one payload, for example a list of nodes and run ids, or document that this is intended.

candidates.title: Visible-range effect is gated on a ref that is not a dependency, so the advertised seam does not activate on the first series
candidates.text:
The effect reads `seriesCountRef.current === 0` as its data guard but lists only `[mount.ready, chart, range]` as dependencies. `seriesCountRef` is a ref (src/chart/use-chart-provider.ts:72), written by `series.onAdded`/`onRemoved` (lines 147–151); writing it does not re-render and cannot re-run an effect. So when the count goes 0 → 1 while `range` is unchanged, the effect does not re-run and `chart.setVisibleRange(range)` is never issued.

The comment at lines 328–338 asserts "The effect and its dependency array stay wired as the seam initiative 120 activates the moment it adds the first series." That is not what the code does: it activates on the *next* range change after a series exists. The initiative-120 flow this seam is built for (range set → data fetched → `addSeries`) would therefore apply the range only if the range happens to change again afterwards. The test that appears to cover this, `src/test/use-chart-provider.translation.test.tsx:135-145` ("applies the range once a series exists"), passes only because it calls `setRange` *after* `addSeries` — it exercises the incidental ordering, not the claim in the comment. The current-slice behaviour is still correct (the chart is empty by design, so the call is always withheld), which is why this is a CONCERN rather than a FAIL.

candidates.title: The visible-range seam does not activate when a series is added, contrary to its comment
candidates.text: The comment states "the effect and its dependency array stay wired as the seam initiative 120 activates the moment it adds the first series." That is not what the code does. The guard reads `seriesCountRef.current` (line 341) inside an effect whose dependencies are `[mount.ready, chart, range]` (line 345). `series.onAdded`/`onRemoved` in `src/chart/chart-facade.ts:47-56` mutate the ref only — no render, no effect re-run — so adding a series changes nothing; the range is applied only on the next `range` change (or a remount). The covering test "applies the range once a series exists" (`src/test/use-chart-provider.translation.test.tsx`) actually passes *because* it also calls `setRange` afterwards, and its `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` assertion confirms the effect did not run at `addSeries` time. So a future consumer that adds a series and expects the Context's default range to be applied will silently get the library's auto-fit. The comment should say the effect fires on the next range change, or the count should become render-visible state if activation-on-add is intended.

candidates.title: Visible range is not applied after a series is added
candidates.text: The range effect depends on `[mount.ready, chart, range]`. Adding a series through the facade changes none of these, so the effect does not re-run. The comment at lines 333-338 says the seam activates "the moment it adds the first series," which the code does not do. The test at `src/test/use-chart-provider.translation.test.tsx:135` passes only because it calls `setRange` after `addSeries`. Reverse the order and the range is never applied. The container is the `section` with the `border` class (`src/routes/chart-route.tsx:92`), and `theme.css` imports Tailwind, which sets `box-sizing: border-box`. Reading the CSS, the first `resize` passes 640px for a box whose content is 638px, and the observer corrects it when it first fires. The impact is probably transient and never painted. Still, the comment at lines 243-248 says the chart matches its container on first paint, and the code does not guarantee that. Use one measurement source for both paths. I did not run the app to confirm the pixel values.

The comment at lines 333-338 says the effect "activates the moment it adds the first series." That is false. A range set before the first series is never applied until the range changes again. The test "applies the range once a series exists" in `src/test/use-chart-provider.translation.test.tsx` adds the series before calling `setRange`, which hides the gap. The test named "keeps the first error rather than being reset by a later success" in `src/test/use-chart-provider.errors.test.tsx` has one failure and one success. candidates.text: `runGuarded` returns `undefined` when the provider is null, with no log and no state change. The mount effect also returns silently when `containerRef.current` is null (lines 168-171), and the lifecycle test "does nothing when the container ref is null" asserts that silence. candidates.title: Range translation is not applied when the first series is added after the range is set
candidates.text:
The visible-range effect depends on `[mount.ready, chart, range]`. The series count lives in `seriesCountRef` (line 72), which is a ref. `addSeries` through the facade increments it (`src/chart/chart-facade.ts:49-56`) but triggers no render, so the effect does not re-run. If the Context range is set while the chart is empty, the effect returns early at line 341. When the first series is added later, nothing re-runs the effect, so the current range is not applied until the range changes again.

The comment at lines 337-338 says the seam "activates the moment it adds the first series." That is not what happens. The test `use-chart-provider.translation.test.tsx:135-145` passes only because it adds the series before calling `setRange`. Its comment at lines 166-167 shows the ordering was chosen on purpose. No test covers "range set, then first series added," which is the case initiative 120 will hit first. candidates.title: Calls made before the chart is live are dropped silently
candidates.text: `runGuarded` returns `undefined` when `providerRef.current` is null or `disposedRef` is set. It does not log and does not change state. The comment at lines 101-107 justifies the drop only for the torn-down case. Before mount, the drop is silent too. React runs child effects before the parent's effect, so a child that calls `chart.addSeries(...)` from its own mount effect has the call dropped, and nothing in `error` or `ready` reports it. candidates.title: The "inert after teardown" tests cannot fail
candidates.text:
The hook's subscription handlers (`src/chart/use-chart-provider.ts:286-301`) have a body that is only `if (disposedRef.current) { return }`. They never call the provider, never resize, and never read a range. The test "makes a subscription callback fired after teardown inert" checks that the handlers don't throw, that `getVisibleRange` isn't called, and that `resize` ran once. Removing the guard changes none of those, so the test passes either way. It gives false coverage for the teardown race.

The comment at lines 276-278 says they exist to prove the disposer lifecycle under React, so production mounts subscriptions only to exercise them in tests.
